parts.markdown:
Use our free **Georgia paycheck calculator** to estimate your take-home salary after federal income tax, Georgia state income tax, Social Security, Medicare and other payroll deductions.

Enter your annual salary or hourly wage, choose your pay frequency and provide your withholding information to understand how much money you could receive on payday.

Whether you work in Atlanta, Savannah, Augusta, Columbus or another Georgia community, knowing your estimated net earnings can help you evaluate job offers, manage expenses and establish realistic savings goals.

## How to Use the Georgia Paycheck Calculator

Select annual salary if you receive fixed compensation or hourly wage if your earnings depend on working hours.

Enter your gross income before taxes and select the number of paychecks you typically receive each year.

Enter federal and Georgia income tax withheld for the pay period from your pay stub.

Include any retirement contributions, health insurance premiums and additional tax withholding requested from your employer.

Review the individual tax deductions and estimated net paycheck.

If your earnings change during the year, update the calculator inputs to understand how those changes could affect your take-home pay.

## Georgia Payroll Taxes in 2026

Georgia employees generally pay federal and state income taxes alongside ordinary federal payroll contributions.

Georgia's individual income tax rate is 4.99% for the 2026 tax year.

Your actual paycheck withholding depends on the official employer calculation procedures, taxable wages and applicable withholding elections.

Review the [Georgia Department of Revenue's Employer's Tax Guide](https://dor.georgia.gov/employers-tax-guide) for current withholding information.

## How Georgia State Income Tax Works

Georgia uses a flat individual income tax rate. Unlike a progressive tax system, this structure applies the same statutory rate to applicable taxable net income.

However, the amount of taxable income may differ from your gross salary.

## Understanding Georgia Form G-4

Georgia employees generally provide their employers with state withholding information using Form G-4.

The form helps employers determine the applicable withholding status, allowances and additional amounts requested by the employee.

Your Georgia withholding information is separate from your federal Form W-4.

If you start a new job, experience a change in household income or want additional state tax withheld, reviewing your G-4 information may help align withholding with your expected annual tax liability.

Access the form through the [Georgia employer withholding resources](https://dor.georgia.gov/taxes/withholding-tax-employers).

Keep in mind that reducing paycheck withholding does not automatically reduce the final amount of income tax you owe.

## Federal Payroll Taxes for Georgia Employees

### Federal income tax

Federal income tax withholding depends on your taxable earnings, filing status, pay frequency and Form W-4 adjustments.

A worker with multiple jobs may need different withholding settings from someone receiving income from a single employer.

Dependents, qualifying deductions and additional income can also affect federal withholding.

The [IRS federal income tax withholding methods](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15t) provide the official calculation procedures.

### Social Security tax

For 2026, employees generally pay 6.2% of covered Social Security wages, subject to an annual taxable wage ceiling of $184,500.

An employee earning $2,000 in covered wages who has not reached the annual ceiling would contribute $124.

### Medicare tax

Employees generally pay 1.45% of covered Medicare wages.

There is no standard annual wage ceiling for ordinary Medicare withholding.

Employers also generally withhold an additional 0.9% on covered Medicare earnings exceeding $200,000 paid by that employer during the calendar year.

Your final Additional Medicare Tax liability may depend on your filing status.

## Georgia Paycheck Example: $72,000 Salary

Consider an employee earning $72,000 per year before taxes and deductions.
Assume the employee receives $3,000 semimonthly and has not reached any applicable federal payroll contribution thresholds.

The employee would have $2,770.50 remaining before federal income tax, Georgia income tax and other payroll deductions.

To illustrate Georgia's annual income tax structure separately, suppose a single filer has $72,000 of applicable income before the standard deduction and no other adjustments, exemptions or credits.

Subtracting the $15,000 standard deduction leaves $57,000.

Applying the 4.99% annual tax rate produces an illustrative amount of $2,844.30.

This annual example is not a complete state income tax return calculation and should not be used as a substitute for official paycheck withholding schedules.

Use the calculator with your actual G-4 information to estimate your paycheck.

## Does Georgia Have Local Income Taxes?

Georgia generally does not impose separate municipal employee wage income taxes.

This means employees working in Atlanta, Savannah or other Georgia cities generally do not encounter the same type of municipal payroll income taxes found in certain Ohio and Michigan communities.

However, Georgia residents still pay applicable state and federal income taxes.

Other local taxes, including sales taxes and property taxes, can affect the cost of living without appearing as personal wage income tax deductions on your paycheck.

When comparing employment opportunities across Georgia, housing, transportation and benefit expenses may have a greater direct impact on disposable income than municipal income tax differences.

## Georgia Hourly Paycheck Calculator

Hourly employees can estimate gross earnings using their hourly wage and working hours.

Consider a worker earning $24 per hour who works 40 regular hours and eight qualifying overtime hours at time-and-a-half.

Regular earnings:

$24 × 40 = $960

Overtime earnings:

$24 × 1.5 × 8 = $288

Total gross earnings:

$1,248

Applicable taxes and deductions are then calculated using the relevant taxable wage amounts.

Employees in industries such as healthcare, logistics, hospitality and manufacturing may receive irregular earnings because of overtime, shift differentials or bonuses.

Review the [US Department of Labor overtime rules](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime) for information about overtime eligibility.

Recent federal and Georgia tax provisions may affect the annual tax treatment of certain qualifying overtime compensation and tips. These provisions do not mean all overtime earnings or tips are automatically free from paycheck withholding or payroll taxes.

## How Retirement and Health Benefits Affect Take-Home Pay

Retirement contributions and health insurance premiums can significantly influence your net paycheck.

Traditional 401(k) contributions generally provide current federal income tax benefits, while Roth 401(k) contributions use after-income-tax earnings.

Qualifying health insurance arrangements may reduce certain taxable wage amounts.

Other deductions, such as voluntary insurance or retirement contributions made after taxes, may reduce take-home pay without reducing all applicable taxes.

Understanding these differences is important when comparing salary offers.

An employer offering lower insurance premiums or a larger retirement match may provide better overall compensation even when the gross salary is similar to competing offers.

## Comparing Job Offers in Atlanta and Other Georgia Cities

Georgia's employment opportunities span industries including technology, finance, healthcare, transportation and manufacturing.

When comparing job offers, consider more than annual salary.

For instance, increasing your salary from $60,000 to $70,000 adds approximately $833.33 in gross monthly income.

Your actual improvement in spending power will depend on taxes, benefit deductions, commuting costs and other expenses.

A position in metropolitan Atlanta may involve different housing and transportation costs than employment in a smaller Georgia community.

Calculate your estimated take-home pay for each opportunity, then compare how much money remains after essential expenses.

## Planning Your Budget Using Georgia Take-Home Pay

Create a monthly spending plan based on net earnings rather than your gross annual salary.

Start with housing, utilities, food, transportation, healthcare and required debt payments.

Next, determine how much you can realistically contribute toward emergency savings and retirement.

If you receive biweekly paychecks, consider how months containing three paydays could support additional savings or debt repayments.

Our [emergency fund calculator](/savings/emergency-fund-calculator/) can help you evaluate your savings target. Our [loan payment](/calculators/loan-calculator/) and [debt-to-income ratio](/debt/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator/) calculators can help you understand how existing borrowing commitments affect financial flexibility.

If your household or employment situation changes, review your withholding using the [IRS Tax Withholding Estimator](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/tax-withholding-estimator) and the applicable Georgia withholding guidance.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is Georgia's state income tax rate in 2026?

Georgia's individual income tax rate is 4.99% for the 2026 tax year. Actual paycheck withholding depends on the state's official payroll procedures and your withholding information.

### Does Atlanta have a separate employee income tax?

Atlanta generally does not impose a separate municipal personal wage income tax. Employees still pay applicable Georgia and federal taxes.

### How much will I take home from a $70,000 salary in Georgia?

Your net salary depends on filing status, withholding elections, payroll frequency, retirement contributions and other deductions. Enter $70,000 into the Georgia paycheck calculator with your actual information for a personalized estimate.
